passages.lr-001: Countries that host large numbers of international conferences report higher levels of foreign direct investment than countries that host few. A department official has concluded that bidding aggressively to host international conferences is an effective strategy for attracting foreign investment.
passages.lr-002: The trade ministry's new export credit program was launched in January. Export volumes in the following six months were 12 percent higher than in the same period the previous year. The ministry has cited these figures as evidence that the program is working.
passages.lr-003: Every country that has successfully reduced its infant mortality rate below 10 per thousand has achieved near-universal access to prenatal care. Country X has near-universal access to prenatal care.
passages.lr-004: A development agency evaluated two literacy programs. Program A was implemented in twelve districts and produced an average gain of 8 percentage points in adult literacy. Program B was implemented in three districts and produced an average gain of 14 points. The agency's director has recommended discontinuing Program A in favor of expanding Program B nationwide.
passages.lr-005: Diplomatic historians note that alliances formed during peacetime tend to last longer than alliances formed during active hostilities. One historian argues that this is because peacetime alliances are negotiated without the time pressure that distorts wartime bargaining.
passages.lr-006: The finance minister argued that the country should not adopt capital controls, since every country in the region that has adopted them has experienced slower growth over the subsequent decade than countries that did not.
passages.lr-007: A survey of returning exchange program participants found that 78 percent reported a more favorable view of the host country than they had held before the exchange. The program's administrators concluded that the exchange program successfully improves participants' attitudes toward the host country.
passages.lr-008: The embassy's public affairs section increased its social media output by 40 percent last year. Over the same period, favorable mentions of the embassy in local media declined by 15 percent. The section chief concluded that increased social media activity had alienated local journalists.
passages.lr-009: All states that have ratified the convention are required to submit annual compliance reports. Some states that submit annual compliance reports have not ratified the convention.
passages.lr-010: An analyst argues that economic sanctions rarely change the behavior of authoritarian governments, noting that in the past thirty years, only four of forty sanctions regimes targeting authoritarian states produced the policy change sought by the sanctioning countries.
passages.lr-011: A consular officer observes that applicants who arrive at the interview with extensive documentation are refused less often than applicants who arrive with minimal documentation. She concludes that advising applicants to bring more documentation would reduce the refusal rate.
passages.lr-012: The commission's report states that no country has ever transitioned to democracy while experiencing hyperinflation. Country Y is currently experiencing hyperinflation.
passages.lr-013: A policy adviser argues that increasing the size of the diplomatic service would improve the quality of reporting from overseas posts, because posts with more reporting officers currently produce cables that are rated more highly by Washington consumers.
passages.lr-014: Two neighboring countries signed a border agreement in 1998. Border incidents between them fell by 80 percent over the following decade. A regional expert cites this as evidence that formal border agreements reduce interstate friction.

passages.lr-016: Whenever the central bank has raised interest rates by more than two percentage points in a single year, the currency has appreciated against the dollar within six months. The central bank has just announced a rate increase of two and a half points.
passages.lr-017: A researcher finds that countries with more independent judiciaries attract more foreign investment. She also finds that countries with more independent judiciaries tend to have higher per capita income. She concludes that judicial independence causes foreign investment.
passages.lr-018: The director of a humanitarian organization argues that his agency should concentrate its resources in the three countries with the greatest measured need, since concentrating resources produces greater impact per dollar than spreading them across many countries.
passages.lr-019: Officials at a border crossing report that smuggling attempts fell sharply after new scanning equipment was installed. Critics note that smuggling attempts at a nearby crossing without new equipment fell by a similar amount over the same period.
passages.lr-020: A negotiator argues that his counterpart's refusal to discuss the fisheries annex demonstrates that the counterpart's government considers the fisheries issue unimportant.
passages.lr-021: An economist observes that in every year since 2005, countries receiving the largest volumes of development assistance have had the lowest growth rates. He concludes that development assistance impedes economic growth.

questions.stem: The official's reasoning is most vulnerable to which criticism?
choices: It relies on a sample of countries that is too small
It treats a correlation as evidence of a causal relationship in a particular direction
It assumes that all foreign investment is beneficial
It fails to define what counts as an international conference
questions.explanation: The official infers that hosting conferences produces investment, but the causation could easily run the other way — countries already attractive to investors are the ones chosen as conference venues. Options {{2,3}} raise questions that would not rescue the inference even if answered.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the ministry's conclusion?
choices: The program's administrative costs exceeded initial projections
Regional export volumes rose an average of 14 percent over the same period in countries with no such program
Some exporters were unaware the program existed
The program will require reauthorization next year
questions.explanation: If comparable countries without the program saw larger gains, the 12 percent increase looks like a regional trend rather than a program effect. Administrative costs and reauthorization say nothing about whether exports rose because of the program, and low awareness would arguably make the gain more impressive, not less.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country X has reduced its infant mortality rate below 10 per thousand
Country X will eventually reduce its infant mortality rate below 10 per thousand
Country X may or may not have reduced its infant mortality below 10 per thousand
Country X has not reduced its infant mortality rate below 10 per thousand
questions.explanation: The stimulus makes prenatal care a necessary condition for low infant mortality, not a sufficient one. Knowing X satisfies the necessary condition tells us nothing about whether it achieved the outcome — affirming the consequent is the error option {{0}} commits.

questions.stem: Which most seriously undermines the director's recommendation?
choices: Program B was implemented in districts selected for their existing educational infrastructure
Program A was more expensive per participant than Program B
Both programs were evaluated by the same team
Adult literacy is difficult to measure precisely
questions.explanation: If B's three districts were chosen for favorable conditions, its larger gain reflects selection rather than program quality, and nationwide expansion would not replicate it. Cost per participant would strengthen the recommendation, and measurement difficulty affects both programs equally.

questions.stem: The historian's explanation assumes which of the following?
choices: Peacetime alliances are always negotiated by more experienced diplomats
Time pressure during wartime negotiations produces terms that make alliances less durable
Wartime alliances are never renegotiated after hostilities end
Alliance duration is the best measure of alliance effectiveness
questions.explanation: The explanation requires a link between time pressure and reduced durability; without it, the observation about pressure would not explain the difference in longevity. Option {{3}} addresses whether duration is worth caring about, which is a separate question from whether the explanation holds.

questions.stem: The minister's argument is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Capital controls may have been adopted precisely by countries already facing economic difficulties
Some countries outside the region have adopted capital controls successfully
Growth is not the only measure of economic performance
The minister has a personal interest in the outcome
questions.explanation: This is reverse causation dressed as a policy lesson: countries in trouble adopt controls, so the controls may be a marker of prior distress rather than its cause. Option {{3}} is an ad hominem that does not engage the evidence at all.

questions.stem: The administrators' conclusion is most vulnerable because:
choices: The survey relies on participants' self-reported change in attitude, which may not reflect actual change
78 percent is not a large enough majority
The survey did not include participants who withdrew from the program
Favorable attitudes may not persist over time
questions.explanation: Self-reports of attitude change are subject to social desirability and reconstructive memory: participants know what answer the program wants. Options {{2,3}} identify genuine limitations, but the retrospective self-report problem goes to whether the reported change occurred at all.

questions.stem: The section chief's reasoning is flawed primarily because it:
choices: Assumes that a temporal correlation establishes causation without considering other explanations
Relies on an unrepresentative sample of local media
Confuses favorable mentions with favorable attitudes
Overstates the importance of social media
questions.explanation: Two things changed in the same period, and the chief assumes one caused the other. A major bilateral dispute, a change in local media ownership, or a rival government's information campaign would explain the decline equally well.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly inferred?
choices: Some states that have not ratified the convention are nonetheless required to submit reports
Submitting an annual compliance report is not sufficient to establish that a state has ratified the convention
All states that submit reports have ratified the convention
Most states that submit reports have not ratified the convention
questions.explanation: If some reporting states have not ratified, then reporting cannot establish ratification. Option {{0}} adds an unsupported claim about requirement — those states may report voluntarily — and 'most' in option {{3}} goes far beyond 'some.'

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's argument?
choices: The four successful cases all involved sanctions imposed by a single country
In the thirty-six unsuccessful cases, the targeted governments made no policy concessions of any kind
Sanctions imposed on democratic governments succeed at a similar rate
Sanctions regimes are typically maintained for several years
questions.explanation: The claim is that sanctions 'rarely change behavior.' Confirming that the thirty-six failures involved no concessions at all forecloses the objection that partial concessions were achieved and undercounted. Option {{2}} would actually weaken the argument by suggesting the outcome has nothing to do with the regime type the analyst emphasizes.

questions.stem: The officer's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Documentation volume may be a marker of applicant circumstances rather than a cause of approval
Some applicants cannot afford to obtain extensive documentation
Reviewing more documentation lengthens interviews
The officer has not specified how much documentation counts as extensive
questions.explanation: Applicants with stable employment, property, and family ties naturally possess more documentation and are also genuinely more likely to qualify — the documentation reflects the underlying situation rather than creating it. Advising weak applicants to bring more paper would not change the situation the paper documents.

questions.stem: Which of the following follows from the commission's statement?
choices: Country Y will never become a democracy
Country Y is not currently transitioning to democracy
Hyperinflation is caused by authoritarian government
Ending hyperinflation would cause Country Y to democratize
questions.explanation: The claim rules out transitioning while hyperinflation persists, so it licenses only a statement about Y's current condition. 'Never' in option {{0}} ignores that hyperinflation can end, and options {{2,3}} invent causal claims the statement does not make.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument depends on assuming that:
choices: Washington consumers rate cables accurately
The higher ratings at larger posts result from staffing levels rather than from characteristics of those posts
All posts produce cables on similar subjects
Reporting quality is the primary purpose of overseas posts
questions.explanation: Larger posts tend to be in more consequential countries and to attract stronger officers, either of which would explain the ratings without any staffing effect. If the ratings reflect those factors, adding officers elsewhere would not reproduce the result.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the expert's inference?
choices: The agreement was never formally ratified by one of the parties
The primary armed group responsible for earlier incidents dissolved in 1999 for unrelated reasons
Border incidents rose slightly in the eleventh year
Other neighboring pairs have signed similar agreements
questions.explanation: An alternative cause arising at almost the same moment would account for the decline without any effect from the agreement. Option {{0}} is closer to irrelevant than it appears — an unratified agreement that nonetheless preceded a drop in incidents leaves the correlation intact.

questions.stem: The department's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: Bribery may have declined for reasons unrelated to the reforms
The reforms may have reduced reporting of bribery rather than bribery itself
Thirty percent is a modest reduction
Some officials may have opposed the reforms
questions.explanation: The evidence measures reports, not incidents. Anticorruption reforms that intimidate potential complainants or dismantle reporting channels would produce this exact number while corruption continued unchanged. Option {{0}} is a real alternative but a weaker one, since it grants that bribery actually fell.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The currency will certainly appreciate within six months
The currency has appreciated in every past instance meeting this condition, so appreciation is likely but not guaranteed
The central bank raised rates in order to strengthen the currency
Rate increases below two points never cause appreciation
questions.explanation: A perfect past record supports an inductive expectation, not a certainty — the stimulus describes what has happened, not a law. Option {{3}} commits the classic error of inferring that the absence of a stated condition implies the absence of the outcome.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is most vulnerable because:
choices: Her sample of countries is not specified
Per capita income may be a common cause of both judicial independence and investment
Foreign investment is difficult to measure consistently
Judicial independence is not the only determinant of investment
questions.explanation: The researcher herself identifies a third variable correlated with both, which is exactly the structure of a confound. Option {{3}} is true but harmless — a cause need not be the only cause to be a cause.

questions.stem: The director's argument assumes that:
choices: The three countries with greatest measured need can absorb concentrated resources effectively
Other organizations will cover the remaining countries
Measured need is the same as actual need
Donors will approve the reallocation
questions.explanation: The premise that concentration produces greater impact per dollar holds only if the concentrated resources can be productively used; in a country with no delivery capacity, additional funds produce nothing. Options {{1,3}} concern the decision's desirability and feasibility rather than the validity of the reasoning.

questions.stem: The critics' observation functions in the argument by:
choices: Providing a control case suggesting the decline had a common external cause
Demonstrating that the scanning equipment was defective
Showing that smuggling has shifted to other routes
Proving that the officials misreported their figures
questions.explanation: A comparable site without the intervention showing the same change is precisely what a control group is for: it isolates whatever affected both. The critics have not shown the equipment failed, only that the decline is unexplained by it.

questions.stem: The negotiator's inference is questionable because:
choices: Refusal to discuss an issue is at least as consistent with regarding it as too important to concede
The counterpart may lack authority to discuss the annex
Fisheries agreements are usually negotiated separately
The negotiator has misread the counterpart's tone
questions.explanation: Silence supports opposite readings: a party may decline to discuss an issue because it does not matter, or because it matters so much that any discussion risks concession. Option {{1}} is also a live alternative, but the first directly reverses the negotiator's specific inference about importance.

questions.stem: The economist's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that:
choices: Assistance is typically directed toward countries already growing slowly
Growth rates are volatile from year to year
Some assistance is humanitarian rather than developmental
The comparison group is not specified
questions.explanation: Development assistance is allocated on the basis of need, so the poorest and slowest-growing countries receive the most. That allocation rule alone produces the observed pattern with no causal effect of aid whatsoever — an especially clean case of reverse causation.

questions.stem: If the staff association's claim is accurate, the department's evidence is flawed because:
choices: The reduction reflects a change in what is measured rather than in service delivery
Processing time is not a good measure of service quality
The staff association is a biased source
Twenty-five percent is not a large improvement
questions.explanation: Removing the slowest cases from the denominator lowers the average without accelerating anything. This is the canonical form of measurement gaming: the metric improves while the underlying performance is unchanged or worse.

questions.stem: The political scientist's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Assumes effectiveness requires compliance even when compliance is costly
Does not specify which organizations are meant
Ignores the role of great powers in shaping resolutions
Relies on anecdotal evidence
questions.explanation: The argument defines effectiveness so demandingly that only an organization able to compel costly compliance could qualify. Organizations may be effective by coordinating expectations, supplying information, or reducing the cost of agreement — functions the argument's standard renders invisible.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be concluded?
choices: Officer Chen has served in the region previously
Officer Chen is a senior officer
Nothing can be concluded about Officer Chen's background from the information given
Officer Chen is not a senior officer
questions.explanation: The premise says all region-experienced senior officers support the initiative; it does not say only they do. Chen's support is compatible with any background — inferring experience from support is affirming the consequent.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the evaluator's observation?
choices: Institutional reform projects are not worth funding
The donor's two-year requirement systematically disadvantages institutional reform projects
Measurable outcomes are a poor evaluation standard
Projects should be evaluated after seven years
questions.explanation: A requirement to show results in two years cannot be met by work whose results appear in five to seven, so such projects are excluded by the rule's structure rather than by their merit. Option {{0}} draws the opposite lesson from the same facts, and the third and fourth generalize well beyond what was stated.

questions.stem: The trade representative's argument assumes that:
choices: Increased total exports outweigh any losses from increased imports
Imports will not increase at all
The affected sectors will find new employment quickly
The agreement will be ratified
questions.explanation: 'Benefit the country' is a net claim, so it requires that export gains exceed import-related losses. Option {{1}} overstates the assumption — the representative need not deny that imports rise, only that the balance is favorable.

questions.stem: The training director's inference is questionable because:
choices: The officers who reach the highest proficiency may differ systematically in ability or ambition
Language proficiency tests are imperfect measures
Promotion rates vary by cone and grade
Not all posts require language proficiency
questions.explanation: Reaching the highest proficiency level is itself an achievement that selects for aptitude and diligence — the same qualities that drive promotion. The correlation may reflect who completes the training rather than any effect of the training.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The proposed convention will be effectively enforced
The proposed convention satisfies a necessary condition for effective enforcement
The proposed convention is more likely to be enforced than convention without such a mechanism
Dispute-resolution mechanisms guarantee enforcement
questions.explanation: The premise establishes the mechanism as necessary, and the convention has it — that is all that follows. Option {{2}} is a plausible real-world judgment but not a logical entailment: necessary conditions say nothing about comparative probability.

questions.stem: The official's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Treats a small number of past successes as guaranteeing future performance
Fails to define what counts as a crisis
Assumes preventive action is always available
Ignores the cost of maintaining the system
questions.explanation: Three successes are weak evidence about the next case, particularly since crises that were missed entirely would not appear in the record. Option {{2}} identifies a separate gap — between detection and action — that the official's conclusion also glosses over, but the inductive leap is the primary flaw.

questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is flawed because it:
choices: Infers motive from consequence
Relies on approval ratings of uncertain accuracy
Assumes the public was aware of the expulsion
Ignores the ambassador's conduct
questions.explanation: That an action produced a benefit does not establish that the benefit was its purpose. The expulsion may have been a genuine response to the ambassador's conduct, with the rating increase an unanticipated by-product — option {{3}} gestures at this but describes an omission rather than naming the logical error.

questions.stem: The most serious problem with the report's conclusion is that:
choices: Performance ratings are subjective
Voluntary participation means participants may have been higher performers to begin with
The program may have been too short
Officers who declined may have had legitimate reasons
questions.explanation: Self-selection destroys the comparison: officers motivated enough to volunteer for optional training are plausibly the ones who would have rated well regardless. The final sentence about voluntary participation is placed there precisely as the signal.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument assumes that:
choices: Accommodating additional interests necessarily consumes additional time
Bilateral negotiations always succeed
Multilateral negotiations produce worse outcomes
All parties to a multilateral negotiation have distinct interests
questions.explanation: The argument moves from 'more interests' to 'slower,' which requires the link that accommodation takes time. Option {{3}} is close but weaker: even if some parties share interests, the argument survives so long as accommodation is time-consuming.

questions.stem: The economist's response weakens the minister's argument by:
choices: Denying that strategic vulnerability exists
Introducing a cost that must be weighed against the claimed security benefit
Showing that domestic production is technically infeasible
Demonstrating that foreign suppliers are reliable
questions.explanation: The economist does not dispute the vulnerability; he prices the remedy. A 40 percent cost premium converts the minister's one-sided claim into a trade-off requiring justification, which is a weakening move rather than a refutation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the historical records described?
choices: The Vienna settlement eliminated warfare in the nineteenth century
The settlement's peace applied to relations among its participants rather than to their external conduct
European powers were more powerful than non-European societies
Wars outside Europe were caused by the settlement
questions.explanation: The pattern — rare wars within the club, frequent wars outside it — supports a scoped rather than a general peace. Option {{2}} may be historically true but is not what the described distribution of wars establishes.

questions.stem: The study's recommendation is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Officers who remain four years may be assigned to posts where such tours are offered for reasons that also affect reporting quality
Insight is difficult to measure
Longer tours are unpopular with officers
Some officers request extensions
questions.explanation: Four-year tours are not randomly distributed; they cluster at particular posts and are often granted to officers with strong local knowledge or language ability. Either factor would produce better reporting independent of tour length.

questions.stem: The ministry's argument depends on assuming that:
choices: A stable debt-to-GDP ratio indicates sustainability regardless of its level or the terms of the debt
GDP will continue to grow
Other countries maintain similar ratios
The debt is denominated in domestic currency
questions.explanation: Stability alone says nothing about sustainability: a stable ratio financed by short-term foreign-currency debt at high interest is far more fragile than the same ratio in long-dated domestic bonds. Options {{1,3}} are among the specific factors the blanket assumption ignores.

questions.stem: The observer's reasoning is flawed because:
choices: Mutual accusation is evidence about what the parties claim, not about what they did
Ceasefire violations are difficult to verify
One party may be more credible than the other
International monitors were not present
questions.explanation: Both sides accusing each other is exactly what one expects whether responsibility is shared or entirely one-sided, since the guilty party has every incentive to accuse. Treating symmetry of claims as symmetry of conduct is a false-balance error.

questions.stem: The program officer's argument assumes that:
choices: The program's value depends on recipients returning home
Seventy percent is an unusually high non-return rate
Recipients who remain abroad provide no benefit to their home countries
questions.explanation: The argument needs both premises: that return is the measure of value, and that non-returners contribute nothing — otherwise remittances, diaspora investment, and professional networks might vindicate the program. Isolating only one assumption leaves the argument intact against the other objection.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country Z has joined the customs union
Country Z has not joined the customs union
Country Z may or may not have joined the customs union
Country Z will join the customs union
questions.explanation: Joining is stated as sufficient for increased trade, not necessary. Z's trade increase is consistent with membership and equally consistent with any number of other causes.

questions.stem: The official's proposal is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Moves from a claim about the strongest single predictor to a policy that ignores all other predictors
Assumes language training is available for all languages
Overlooks the cost of language training
Assumes reporting is the only function of overseas posts
questions.explanation: Being the strongest single predictor is compatible with explaining only a modest share of the outcome, and an assignment rule using one variable discards everything the others contribute. Option {{3}} raises a real limitation, but the statistical overreach is the error in the reasoning itself.

questions.stem: The comparison described is unreliable because:
choices: The two groups of villages differed systematically before the intervention
Health outcomes were self-reported
The follow-up period was too short
Water quality was not measured directly
questions.explanation: Villages with the greatest capacity to maintain infrastructure likely differ in wealth, governance, and baseline health — differences that could produce better outcomes on their own. Non-random assignment on a variable correlated with the outcome is the defining feature of selection bias.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest because it:
choices: Assumes that a policy which has not yet succeeded will not succeed
Ignores the humanitarian costs of sanctions
Fails to identify an alternative policy
Relies on an arbitrary time period
questions.explanation: Absence of results within a chosen interval is not evidence that results will never come, particularly for a policy that works by accumulating pressure. Option {{3}} is closely related and also correct as far as it goes, but the inferential error is treating 'not yet' as 'not.'

questions.stem: The department's use of the poll is problematic because:
choices: The question asked about a broad sentiment rather than the specific agreement
Sixty-two percent is not a supermajority
The sample size is not given
Polls are unreliable predictors of behavior
questions.explanation: Almost everyone favors 'expanding economic cooperation' in the abstract; support for a particular agreement with particular concessions is a different and usually lower number. Inferring specific support from a favorably worded general question is the substitution the department has made.

questions.stem: The analyst's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: A record of no war may reflect deterrence or luck rather than the absence of risk
Sixty years is a short period historically
Other disputes in the region have led to war
The states may have fought undeclared conflicts
questions.explanation: Absence of war is compatible with a dispute held in check by costly deterrence — a situation of high latent risk, not low risk. Reading a quiet record as evidence of safety is precisely the inference that fails when the conditions sustaining the quiet change.

questions.stem: The researcher's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that:
choices: Peacekeeping missions are deployed to countries already experiencing political violence
Political violence is inconsistently defined across countries
Peacekeeping missions vary widely in size and mandate
Some missions have lasted decades
questions.explanation: Missions are sent where violence is worst, so the correlation is built into the deployment decision. The relevant comparison is not peacekept versus peaceful countries but how violent countries with missions fare against comparably violent countries without them.

questions.stem: Which principle, if established, would most justify treating the export figures as evidence the program works?
choices: Government programs should be evaluated by their measurable outputs
A change following an intervention may be attributed to it when comparable cases without the intervention show no similar change
Export growth is always desirable
Programs should be given at least a year before evaluation
questions.explanation: The principle supplies the missing comparative condition that would license the causal attribution. Option {{0}} would justify measuring something but not attributing it, and the other two are policy preferences with no bearing on inference.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the director's recommendation?
choices: Humanitarian organizations should distribute resources equitably across all countries in need
An organization should allocate resources so as to maximize total impact, even at the cost of leaving some needs unaddressed
Organizations should follow donor preferences in allocating resources
Need should be measured by objective indicators rather than by political salience
questions.explanation: The recommendation trades breadth for intensity, which only a maximizing principle justifies. Option {{0}} supports the opposite policy, and the fourth addresses how to measure need rather than how to allocate against it.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the training director's conclusion?
choices: Officers assigned to the training by lottery were promoted at higher rates than those not assigned
The training program has been offered for over a decade
Officers report finding the training valuable
Language-designated positions are more numerous than they once were
questions.explanation: Random assignment eliminates the self-selection problem that makes the original correlation ambiguous, so a promotion gap under lottery assignment is direct evidence of an effect. Subjective reports of value and program longevity say nothing about the causal question.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the officer's conclusion?
choices: Applicants who brought extensive documentation were also more likely to own property and hold long-term employment
Documentation requirements are published on the embassy website
Some approved applicants brought no documentation at all
Interview length correlates with documentation volume
questions.explanation: This names the confound explicitly: the documentation is a downstream marker of the ties that actually drive approval. Option {{2}} is weaker — a few exceptions do not undermine a general pattern, whereas an identified common cause explains the whole pattern away.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most strongly supported?
choices: The donor's portfolio will underrepresent institutional reform work relative to its share of identified need
Institutional reform projects produce larger benefits than other projects
The donor should extend its requirement to seven years
Evaluators disagree with donors about project value
questions.explanation: If a funding rule filters out a category of project by timeline rather than merit, that category will be underrepresented relative to need — an inference that follows from the two stated facts alone. Options {{1,2}} make evaluative claims the stimulus does not support.

questions.stem: The economist's conclusion requires the assumption that:
choices: Assistance levels are not determined by the recipient's growth performance
All assistance is delivered as direct budget support
Growth is measured consistently across countries
Countries receiving assistance would otherwise receive private investment
questions.explanation: The causal claim collapses if aid volumes are set by prior growth performance, since the correlation would then be an artifact of the allocation rule. Option {{2}} concerns data quality — a real issue, but not what the causal inference depends on.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?
choices: Countries with missions and comparably violent countries without missions show identical trajectories of violence
Peacekeeping missions are expensive to maintain
Some missions have been withdrawn before their mandates expired
Host governments sometimes object to mission deployments
questions.explanation: Matching on baseline violence removes the selection problem, so identical trajectories would genuinely indicate no effect. Cost, early withdrawal, and host objections all speak to the politics of missions rather than to whether they reduce violence.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the energy minister's position over the economist's?
choices: Economic efficiency should govern all decisions about industrial policy
A state should accept economic costs to reduce dependence on suppliers it cannot control
Domestic industries should be protected from foreign competition
Energy prices should be set by the market
questions.explanation: The minister needs a principle that makes security worth paying for, which is exactly what this states. Option {{2}} is broader protectionism, which would support the conclusion but on grounds the minister never invoked — and the question asks which principle supports his position, not merely his conclusion.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: The next crisis will resemble the previous three in ways relevant to detection
The early-warning system is operated by trained analysts
Preventive action always succeeds when taken
No crises have been missed by the system
questions.explanation: An induction from past cases holds only if the next case is relevantly similar; a novel crisis type could evade a system tuned to familiar signatures. Option {{3}} would strengthen the argument if true but is not something the argument must assume.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most undermines the historian's explanation?
choices: Peacetime alliances are typically formed between states with pre-existing alignment of interests
Wartime alliances often involve more parties
Time pressure affects all negotiations to some degree
Some peacetime alliances have dissolved quickly
questions.explanation: If peacetime allies already share interests, their alliances last longer for that reason — the negotiating conditions become incidental. This is the strongest alternative explanation because it accounts for the full pattern rather than merely qualifying it, as options {{2,3}} do.

questions.stem: If both the department's figure and the staff association's claim are accurate, which is best supported?
choices: Average processing time for the cases still counted has fallen, while overall performance is unknown
The department has deliberately misled the public
Complex cases now take longer than before
Service quality has declined
questions.explanation: Both statements can hold simultaneously: the reported average is genuine for its narrowed population, and nothing is established about the excluded cases. Options {{1,2,3}} all add claims — about intent, about the excluded cases, about quality — that the two facts together do not establish.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the section chief's conclusion?
choices: A major bilateral dispute over fishing rights dominated local coverage during the same period
The embassy's social media following grew during the year
Other embassies in the country also increased social media output
Local journalists rarely use social media professionally
questions.explanation: An intervening event that would independently depress favorable coverage supplies an alternative explanation for the entire decline. Option {{3}} is tempting — it questions the mechanism — but a chief could reply that journalists need not use social media to resent an embassy that has stopped engaging them directly.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most justify abandoning the sanctions regime?
choices: A policy should be abandoned once its costs to the imposing states exceed the value of the change it seeks
Sanctions should never be imposed on countries with which trade is substantial
Policies should be reviewed periodically
A policy that has not achieved its objective within eighteen months will not achieve it
questions.explanation: The commentator's argument turns entirely on the passage of eighteen months, so only a principle connecting that interval to futility justifies the conclusion as argued. Option {{0}} is a more defensible principle but supports a different argument — one about costs, which the commentator never raised.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the information given?
choices: The scanning equipment had no effect on smuggling
The decline in smuggling attempts at the first crossing is not clearly attributable to the equipment
Smuggling has increased overall in the region
The nearby crossing also received new equipment
questions.explanation: A parallel decline without the intervention undercuts the attribution without establishing that the equipment did nothing — it could have contributed alongside whatever affected both sites. Option {{0}} overstates the evidence in the same way the officials overstated theirs.

questions.stem: The department's argument assumes that:
choices: Support for 'expanding economic cooperation' translates into support for this specific agreement
The poll used a representative sample
Respondents understood the question
Public support is necessary for ratification
questions.explanation: The entire inference rests on equating a general sentiment with a specific commitment. Representativeness and comprehension are ordinary polling caveats that would matter even if the question had been perfectly targeted; the substitution of the general for the specific is what this argument uniquely requires.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the study's recommendation?
choices: Personnel policy should be set by the preferences of the officers affected
When a measured difference in output tracks a difference in assignment length, assignment length should be adjusted to favor the better-performing arrangement
Officers should be assigned to posts where their language skills are strongest
Reporting quality should be the primary criterion for evaluating overseas posts
questions.explanation: The recommendation moves from an observed difference to a policy change, which requires a principle licensing exactly that move. Option {{3}} would establish that reporting quality matters but would not justify treating tour length as its cause, and the first would support consulting officers rather than following the data.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the political scientist's conclusion?
choices: An institution is effective only if it can secure compliance that members would not otherwise offer
International organizations should be funded in proportion to their results
States are the primary actors in international politics
Resolutions that are routinely ignored should not be adopted
questions.explanation: The argument treats costly non-compliance as proof of ineffectiveness, which holds only under a standard that equates effectiveness with compelling unwilling behavior. Option {{2}} is a background assumption of the field rather than a principle that connects the evidence to the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: State F has not accepted the optional protocol
State F will accept the protocol in future
State F has violated the protocol
Some states that accepted the protocol do not permit complaints
questions.explanation: All acceptors permit complaints, and F does not, so F cannot be an acceptor — a valid contrapositive. Option {{3}} directly contradicts the first premise.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly concluded?
choices: Addressing a priority sector guarantees funding
Addressing a priority sector is necessary but not sufficient for funding
No projects in priority sectors are funded
The department's criteria are inconsistently applied
questions.explanation: 'Only if' establishes necessity, and the second premise shows the condition can be met without funding following, which rules out sufficiency. Option {{3}} imputes inconsistency where the stimulus describes a rule with additional unstated criteria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: Completing a hardship tour is necessary but not sufficient for promotion
Completing a hardship tour guarantees promotion
Most officers who complete hardship tours are promoted
Promotion requires nothing beyond a hardship tour
questions.explanation: Every promoted officer had a hardship tour, making it necessary; some who had one were not promoted, so it is not sufficient. Option {{2}} makes a quantitative claim the premises cannot support.

questions.stem: Which of the following follows?
choices: The fisheries agreement will not survive a change of government
The fisheries agreement has already collapsed
No agreement survives a change of government
The fisheries agreement was poorly drafted
questions.explanation: The universal claim applies to any agreement reached under time pressure, and the fisheries agreement is one. Option {{1}} adds a timing claim, and the third drops the qualifying condition that makes the premise limited.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The delegation received new instructions
The delegation did not receive new instructions
The delegation will table a revised text later
New instructions were sent but not received
questions.explanation: Denying the consequent of a conditional lets you deny the antecedent. Concluding that instructions were received would affirm the consequent, which is invalid — and here the consequent is denied, not affirmed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: Inflation in Country K has certainly fallen
Inflation in Country K probably fell, though it may not have
Inflation in Country K has not fallen
The reform causes inflation to fall
questions.explanation: 'Most' supports a probabilistic expectation, not a certainty, since K could be among the minority. Option {{3}} asserts causation from an observed association across countries.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be concluded about the new system?
choices: It is effective
It satisfies a condition that all effective systems satisfy
It is more effective than systems lacking political analysis
It will detect the next crisis
questions.explanation: The premise makes the combination necessary for effectiveness, not sufficient, so meeting it establishes eligibility only. Concluding effectiveness affirms the consequent.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: The donor violated its own policy
Meeting targets is necessary for renewal but does not guarantee it
The literacy program did not actually meet its targets
The donor has discontinued all funding
questions.explanation: 'Only for' states a necessary condition, and a program can satisfy it while other unstated considerations block renewal. Treating a necessary condition as sufficient and then alleging a violation is the trap in option {{0}}.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The pending treaty will be ratified
The pending treaty differs from every treaty rejected in the past fifty years in at least one respect
Bipartisan sponsorship guarantees ratification
The Senate has rejected few treaties
questions.explanation: All rejected treaties lacked bipartisan sponsorship and this one has it, so it differs from each of them on that attribute. It does not follow that it will be ratified — treaties can fail for reasons the historical pattern does not capture.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly inferred?
choices: All members of the working group have doctoral degrees
Some members of the working group may have doctoral degrees, but this does not follow necessarily
No members of the working group have doctoral degrees
All economists are members of the working group
questions.explanation: The second premise covers economists in the department, and nothing establishes that the working group's economists are department economists. Without that link, the syllogism does not close — which is exactly what the question tests.

questions.stem: The section's argument assumes that:
choices: The conditions that motivated the previous boycotts still obtain
The opposition is united
The election will be held on schedule
Boycotts are an effective strategy
questions.explanation: Projecting past behavior forward requires that the reasons for it persist; an opposition that boycotted because of a since-repealed law would have no reason to repeat. The absence of an announced change is weaker evidence than the argument treats it as.

questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Treats co-movement as evidence that one variable drives the other
Relies on too few years of data
Ignores imports entirely
Assumes GDP is measured accurately
questions.explanation: Exports are a component of GDP, so the two rising together is close to arithmetic and says nothing about what drives growth. Domestic demand could be the engine with exports merely rising alongside it.

questions.stem: The official's argument depends on the assumption that:
choices: Officers selected for the accelerated program are comparable to those in the standard program
Language training is the department's largest expense
All officers require the same proficiency level
The proficiency test is administered annually
questions.explanation: If accelerated candidates are chosen for prior aptitude, their reaching the same level says nothing about what would happen if everyone were accelerated. The comparison only supports the policy if the two groups are alike.

questions.stem: The researcher's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Adopts a standard of legitimacy that few institutions of any kind could satisfy
Does not identify which courts are meant
Assumes states are unitary actors
Overlooks regional courts
questions.explanation: Compliance when convenient describes most domestic legal compliance as well, so the standard would delegitimize nearly all law. A criterion that proves far too much is not a useful test.

questions.stem: The security adviser's reasoning is flawed because:
choices: The absence of detections is equally consistent with the procedure failing to detect anything
The procedure may be expensive
Prohibited items are rare in any case
The previous procedure also detected nothing
questions.explanation: A screening procedure that detects nothing might be deterring smuggling or might simply be blind. Without an independent measure of what passed through, the evidence cannot distinguish success from failure.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument is most vulnerable because it:
choices: Treats a position's location between two others as establishing that it is reasonable
Assumes the other parties negotiated in good faith
Does not specify the substance of the proposal
Overlooks the possibility of a fourth party
questions.explanation: If both other positions are extreme, the midpoint is extreme too — moderation is not a matter of position on a scale defined by whoever happens to be present. This is the argument-to-moderation fallacy.

questions.stem: The economist's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Employment might have grown absent the increase, so flat employment could conceal a loss
One year is too short a period
The minimum wage affects only some workers
Employment is difficult to measure
questions.explanation: The relevant comparison is against the counterfactual, not against the prior level. If the sector was expanding, unchanged employment represents jobs that would otherwise have existed.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Treats one qualification as though it were the only relevant one
Attacks the ambassador personally
Assumes regional experience can be measured
Ignores the confirmation process
questions.explanation: Regional experience is one input among several — negotiating skill, management ability, access to the President — and its absence does not settle the question. The argument treats a necessary-sounding condition as the whole test.

questions.stem: The official's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: The proposed policy also has serious drawbacks
Some alternatives were not considered
The drawbacks could be mitigated
The policy may be expensive
questions.explanation: Showing that every alternative is flawed does not show the proposal is not, and the proposal may be worse than several of them. A comparative judgment requires evaluating the proposal on the same terms as the alternatives.

questions.stem: The study's recommendation assumes that:
choices: Budget size drives coverage rather than both reflecting the importance of the relationship
Media coverage is accurately measured
All embassies pursue the same objectives
Favorable coverage benefits the sending state
questions.explanation: Large public affairs budgets go to posts in countries the sending state considers important, and those relationships attract favorable coverage for independent reasons. Without ruling that out, increasing budgets elsewhere would not reproduce the result.

questions.stem: The negotiator's inference is questionable because:
choices: Hardening without explanation is consistent with several motives, including tactical ones
Domestic pressure is difficult to observe
The other delegation may lack instructions
Negotiations often involve posturing
questions.explanation: A delegation might harden to extract concessions, to test resolve, or because its own assessment changed. Selecting one explanation from several compatible with the evidence is the error.

questions.stem: The department's evidence is weak primarily because:
choices: Self-reported time estimates may not reflect actual time spent
Officers may dislike the new system
Administrative tasks are hard to define
The system was expensive to install
questions.explanation: Perceptions of time are unreliable and may be shaped by expectations about a new system. An objective measure of hours or throughput would settle the question that self-reports cannot.

questions.stem: The bureau's argument is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Cable volume may not measure the value of a post's work
Other posts may produce excessive cables
Cable counts are recorded inconsistently
The post may be newly opened
questions.explanation: A post may deliver its principal value through consular services, security cooperation, or commercial advocacy, none of which generates reporting volume. Selecting the metric determines the answer, which is why the choice of metric is the vulnerable step.

questions.stem: The adviser's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: Past crises sharing a precursor does not establish that the next will share it
Exchange rates are volatile
Currency data may be unreliable
Three cases is a small sample
questions.explanation: Optimizing surveillance for the last war's indicator leaves a system blind to a crisis with a different origin. Option {{3}} is a weaker version of the same complaint — even thirty cases would not guarantee the next resembles them.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is flawed because:
choices: Public characterization of an agreement is not evidence of intent to implement it
Historic agreements often fail
Only one signatory's view is reported
The agreement may be ambiguous
questions.explanation: Signatories have every incentive to describe an agreement favorably regardless of their commitment to it. Rhetoric at signature is among the weakest available predictors of durability.

questions.stem: The officer's argument assumes that:
choices: Past accuracy predicts current accuracy for this source
The source has no motive to deceive
The information can be independently verified
The source has access to privileged information
questions.explanation: Reliability is being inferred from a single prior instance, which requires that past performance carry forward. A source accurate on one subject may be uninformed or motivated differently on another.

questions.stem: The department's evidence is weakest because:
choices: Alumni who accepted scholarships may have held favorable views beforehand
A decade is too short to assess goodwill
Surveys of alumni are expensive
Not all alumni respond to surveys
questions.explanation: Applicants self-select for interest in the sponsoring country, so favorable views may predate the program entirely. Option {{3}} raises a real but lesser problem — nonresponse bias compounds selection rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: The policy paper's argument is most vulnerable because it:
choices: Identifies a cost of joining without weighing it against any benefit
Overstates the number of statutes affected
Assumes amendments would be controversial
Ignores the views of other parties
questions.explanation: Twelve amendments is a cost, and a decision requires comparing it with what accession would deliver. An argument citing only one side of a ledger cannot support a conclusion about the balance.

questions.stem: The analyst's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Observers visited only a subset of stations, which may not have been representative
Observers may lack local language skills
Irregularities may occur after polls close
International observation is politically contested
questions.explanation: Coverage is the issue: stations chosen for accessibility or safety are systematically different from those where problems are likeliest. Option {{2}} identifies a genuine additional gap but a narrower one.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: Fees should track the cost of providing the service
Applicants can afford a higher fee
Demand will not fall if fees rise
Other posts charge more
questions.explanation: The argument moves from rising costs to a fee increase, which requires a cost-recovery principle. A government could as easily decide that consular services should be subsidized, in which case rising costs would not imply rising fees.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Assumes the two situations are alike in the respects that matter
Relies on only two examples
Does not define coherence
Ignores the role of allies
questions.explanation: Supporting self-determination in one case and territorial integrity in another is inconsistent only if the cases are relevantly similar; differing facts can make different principles apply. Charging incoherence requires establishing the similarity, which the argument skips.

questions.stem: The economist's argument assumes that:
choices: The goods in the basket are genuinely comparable and freely tradable between the two countries
The two countries have similar income levels
Exchange rates are set by governments
The basket includes only manufactured goods
questions.explanation: Purchasing power comparisons require that price differences reflect currency values rather than quality differences or non-tradable services. Haircuts and housing are systematically cheaper in poorer countries for reasons unrelated to overvaluation.

questions.stem: The evaluation's conclusion is flawed because:
choices: Confidence and ability are distinct, and training can raise one without the other
The survey sample was small
Graduates may have forgotten the training
Negotiating ability varies by context
questions.explanation: Self-assessed confidence is a poor proxy for competence and frequently moves in the wrong direction after instruction. An objective performance measure is what the inference requires.

questions.stem: The specialist's argument assumes that:
choices: Both governments will act on a calculation of economic interest
The two economies are equally dependent on trade
War is always economically ruinous
Neither government faces domestic opposition
questions.explanation: The prediction rests on states behaving as rational economic maximizers, which history repeatedly disappoints — governments have gone to war knowing the cost. Identifying a strong disincentive is not the same as identifying a decisive one.

questions.stem: The official's argument commits which error?
choices: Treating already-spent resources as a reason to continue
Assuming the program has no benefits
Confusing correlation with causation
Appealing to popular opinion
questions.explanation: This is the sunk cost fallacy: money already spent cannot be recovered by either continuing or stopping, so it is irrelevant to the forward-looking decision. The only relevant question is whether future benefits exceed future costs.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is most vulnerable because:
choices: Effective governments may permit press freedom rather than the reverse
Press freedom rankings are subjective
Government effectiveness is hard to measure
The sample excludes some countries
questions.explanation: The causal arrow could run either way, or a third factor such as institutional development could produce both. Measurement objections do not resolve the direction problem, which is the argument's central weakness.

questions.stem: The information about application volume weakens the department's claim by suggesting that:
choices: The fraud decline may reflect fewer applications rather than deterrence
The interview requirement was unpopular
Fraudulent applications are hard to detect
Interviews are expensive to conduct
questions.explanation: If applications halved, a fall in fraudulent applications is partly arithmetic. The relevant figure is the fraud rate per application, which the department has not reported.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument assumes that:
choices: The efficiency difference stems from management practices rather than differing objectives and constraints
Private firms measure efficiency accurately
Government agencies resist reform
Performance management is inexpensive to implement
questions.explanation: Agencies pursue goals firms do not — equity, due process, statutory compliance — and are constrained in ways firms are not. If those differences explain the efficiency gap, importing the practices will not close it.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument overlooks that a treaty may:
choices: Lock in current compliance against future change
Be cheaper than domestic legislation
Attract additional signatories
Require periodic review
questions.explanation: Present compliance says nothing about future governments, and binding commitments exist precisely to constrain successors. Treaties also signal credibility to other parties in ways unilateral practice does not.

questions.stem: The analyst's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Power-sharing provisions may be adopted precisely in the most intractable conflicts
Five years is an arbitrary threshold
Some agreements without power-sharing also collapsed
The region may be unrepresentative
questions.explanation: Negotiators reach for power-sharing when a conflict is too divided to resolve otherwise, so the provision may mark difficulty rather than cause failure. Option {{2}} would strengthen the objection but is not asserted.

questions.stem: The department's evidence is weak because:
choices: Knowing the right answer on an assessment differs from behaving accordingly
The assessment may be too easy
Participants may have discussed the answers
Training is expensive
questions.explanation: Ethics assessments measure recognition of correct answers, which participants can supply without any change in conduct — particularly when they know what the trainer wants. The outcome of interest is behavior, which was not measured.

questions.stem: The officer's reasoning is flawed because:
choices: That denials are routine does not establish that this denial is false
The host government may be telling the truth
Denials are sometimes accompanied by evidence
The allegation may itself be unfounded
questions.explanation: A base rate about how governments generally behave cannot settle a particular case, since innocent governments also deny false allegations. Option {{1}} states a possibility; the first identifies why the inference fails.

questions.stem: The specialist's argument assumes that:
choices: The five conditions were not intended to be satisfied jointly before relief
The remaining two conditions are unimportant
The target government acted in good faith
Relief can be reversed if compliance lapses
questions.explanation: If the conditions were framed as a package, partial compliance does not trigger relief however substantial. Option {{1}} is close but stronger than needed — the conditions could matter and still be severable.

questions.stem: The projection is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: The pilot population is unrepresentative of applicants elsewhere
Digitization is expensive
Processing time is hard to measure
Forty percent is an unusually large improvement
questions.explanation: A highly connected urban population will adopt an online system far more readily than rural or less-connected applicants. Generalizing from a favorable pilot site is among the most common errors in program scaling.

questions.stem: The analyst's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: An average tells you little about when any particular coalition will end
Eighteen months is a short average
The parliamentary system may have changed
Coalitions sometimes reform after collapsing
questions.explanation: Exceeding an average is unremarkable — roughly half of all cases do — and says nothing about imminent collapse. Treating a mean as a threshold is the specific error.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is flawed because:
choices: Parties sometimes deliberately avoid a communiqué while still achieving their aims
Communiqués are often drafted in advance
Summits have multiple purposes
Failure is difficult to define
questions.explanation: A summit may aim at private understanding, relationship-building, or avoiding a public commitment, and issuing no document can be the intended outcome. The presence of a communiqué is a weak proxy for success in either direction.

questions.stem: The official's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Treats popularity as establishing that a policy is justified
Overstates the size of the majority
Ignores the views of experts
Assumes the public is well informed
questions.explanation: Popular support may be a reason to adopt a policy in a democracy without establishing that the policy is sound — majorities have endorsed unjust and ineffective measures. The argument conflates political feasibility with justification.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: The road may have been routed through areas that were already better off
Income is difficult to measure in rural areas
The road may be recently built
Distance can be measured in several ways
questions.explanation: Road placement is rarely random; planners follow existing settlement, commerce, and terrain. If routing favored more prosperous areas, the income gap predates the road entirely.

questions.stem: The department's inference is questionable because:
choices: An absence of discipline may reflect weak enforcement rather than good compliance
The standard may be new
Discipline records may be confidential
Officers may be unaware of the standard
questions.explanation: The same record is produced by universal compliance and by no one looking. Option {{3}} is a live alternative but is itself a species of the enforcement problem option {{0}} names.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument is flawed because:
choices: A source's past error does not establish that the present assessment is wrong
Intelligence assessments are inherently uncertain
The previous error may have been minor
Assessments are produced by teams
questions.explanation: Prior error is a reason for scrutiny, not for dismissal; the current assessment must be evaluated on its own evidence. Treating one failure as disqualifying would eliminate every analytic source in existence.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: Parties may withhold objections for tactical reasons or lack authority to object
The consultations were poorly attended
The text may be technically complex
Objections may be raised later
questions.explanation: Silence in consultation is not assent: delegations commonly reserve positions pending instructions or hold objections for a decisive moment. Option {{3}} is a consequence of the first rather than an independent problem.

questions.stem: The economist's argument assumes that:
choices: Interest rates and revenue will not change materially
The debt is denominated in domestic currency
The government has no contingent liabilities
Eight percent is below the regional average
questions.explanation: A current ratio is a snapshot; rising rates at refinancing or falling revenue would change it quickly. Sustainability is a forward-looking judgment, and the argument treats a present figure as if it settled one.

questions.stem: The analyst's inference is most vulnerable because:
choices: Personnel changes may serve purposes other than policy change, such as managing coalition politics
Three ministers is a small number
The replacements may be inexperienced
Reshuffles occur regularly
questions.explanation: Governments replace ministers to satisfy factions, respond to scandal, or refresh public image, all while continuing the same policy. Inferring direction from personnel requires ruling those out.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Assumes bilateral and multilateral approaches are substitutes rather than complements
Does not count the number of agreements
Ignores regional organizations
Relies on recent data only
questions.explanation: States pursue both simultaneously, often using bilateral agreements to implement multilateral commitments. Rising bilateral activity is evidence of multilateral decline only if the two compete, which the argument assumes without arguing.

questions.stem: The official's argument is most vulnerable because:
choices: Attendance measures participation rather than any effect on attitudes or behavior
The events may have been poorly organized
Attendance figures may be inflated
Two years is a short period
questions.explanation: More people in the room is an output, not an outcome; the program's purpose is presumably to shift views or build relationships. Free food will double attendance without advancing either.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the policy paper's conclusion?
choices: A state should not accept international obligations that require substantial changes to domestic law
International conventions should be ratified only by supermajority
Domestic law should be amended only when a court requires it
States should join conventions that most of their neighbors have joined
questions.explanation: The argument rests entirely on the legislative burden, so only a principle making that burden decisive supports it. Option {{3}} would cut in the opposite direction, and the second and third address procedure rather than the substantive trade-off.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's argument?
choices: Decisions should be based on expected future costs and benefits, disregarding expenditures already made
Programs should run for a minimum of five years
Aid decisions should be made by recipient governments
Programs should be evaluated by independent auditors
questions.explanation: This states the standard that makes sunk costs irrelevant, removing the argument's only support. The other options concern process and duration, neither of which touches the reasoning error.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports granting relief?
choices: Partial compliance should be met with proportionate relief to reward progress
Sanctions should be lifted only on full compliance
Sanctions should never be imposed on states that negotiate
Relief decisions should be made multilaterally
questions.explanation: A proportionality principle makes three of five conditions a basis for partial relief, which is what the specialist urges. Option {{1}} states the opposite rule, and the remaining two address who decides rather than on what basis.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the bureau's recommendation?
choices: Posts should be maintained in proportion to their measurable reporting output
Diplomatic presence should be maintained in every country
Resource decisions should be made by the posts themselves
Reporting quality matters more than quantity
questions.explanation: The recommendation turns cable counts into a closure decision, which requires a principle tying presence to that specific output. Option {{3}} would undermine the argument, since it shifts the criterion the bureau relied on.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support shortening the training?
choices: Training should be no longer than required to reach the certified proficiency standard
Training decisions should be made by language instructors
Officers should be consulted about training length
Longer training always produces better outcomes
questions.explanation: A minimum-sufficient-duration principle converts equal outcomes into a case for the shorter program. Option {{3}} contradicts the premise, and the second and third address who decides rather than the criterion.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's argument?
choices: Consular services to citizens abroad should be subsidized rather than priced at cost
Fees should be reviewed every five years
Fee changes require legislative approval
Fees should be comparable across posts
questions.explanation: The argument depends on a cost-recovery premise, so a principle rejecting cost recovery removes its foundation. The other options impose procedural or comparative constraints without touching the underlying rationale.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the study's recommendation?
choices: Where a resource is associated with a desired outcome, increasing the resource is warranted absent evidence of a common cause
Public affairs budgets should be equal across posts
Media coverage should not influence budget decisions
Budgets should be set by host-country conditions
questions.explanation: The recommendation needs a principle licensing the leap from association to intervention, and this one states it while acknowledging the confounding caveat. The other options either oppose the recommendation or bear on a different question.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most weaken the economist's conclusion?
choices: A policy's effect should be assessed against what would have happened otherwise, not against the prior level
Employment statistics should be collected quarterly
Minimum wage policy should be set locally
Labor market effects take at least five years to appear
questions.explanation: Stating the counterfactual standard explicitly is what exposes the flaw in comparing to the prior level. Option {{3}} challenges the timeframe but concedes the comparison method, which is the deeper problem.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most undermines the evaluation's conclusion?
choices: A program's effect on a skill should be measured by performance rather than by self-assessment
Training programs should be evaluated after one year
Participants should not be told the evaluation's purpose
Negotiation cannot be taught in a classroom
questions.explanation: The evaluation rests on self-reported confidence, so a principle requiring performance measurement removes its evidentiary basis. Option {{3}} is a stronger claim that would defeat the program entirely rather than the inference.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the department's projection?
choices: Pilot results may be generalized only to populations resembling the pilot population
Digital systems should be introduced gradually
Projections should be revised annually
Processing time should be measured from application to decision
questions.explanation: The projection extrapolates from an unrepresentative site, and this principle blocks exactly that step. The other options concern implementation pace and measurement conventions, neither of which addresses generalizability.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the commentator's argument?
choices: Binding commitments are valuable when they constrain future governments, not only present ones
Treaties should be negotiated multilaterally
Domestic practice should conform to international standards
Compliance should be independently verified
questions.explanation: The commentator infers from present compliance that a treaty adds nothing, and this principle identifies the value it would add regardless. Option {{3}} supports verification without addressing whether the treaty is needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?
choices: The road's route was determined by terrain constraints unrelated to village prosperity
The road was completed five years ago
Villages near the road have grown in population
Road construction is expensive
questions.explanation: If routing was driven by geology rather than by existing wealth, the selection problem largely disappears and the comparison becomes credible. Population growth is ambiguous — it could be a consequence of the road or of prior prosperity.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department's claim?
choices: Applicants rejected for the scholarship report substantially less favorable views a decade later
The program has operated for thirty years
Alumni are surveyed by an independent contractor
Most alumni return to their home countries
questions.explanation: Near-miss rejected applicants share the self-selection that produced the applicant pool, so a gap between them and recipients isolates the program's effect. Survey independence addresses a different concern and would not resolve selection.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the adviser's claim?
choices: Prohibited items were recovered downstream after passing through the screening point
