The procedure requires additional staff
Similar procedures are used at other facilities
The procedure has been in place for six months
questions.explanation: Items getting through establishes that the absence of detections reflects blindness rather than deterrence. Staffing costs and comparative practice say nothing about whether the procedure detects anything.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's conclusion?
choices: Power-sharing was adopted only in conflicts involving three or more armed factions
Some agreements collapsed after six years
Power-sharing provisions vary in design
The agreements were mediated by different parties
questions.explanation: It identifies the confound directly: the provision marks conflicts that were harder to settle for independent reasons. Design variation and differing mediators are potential noise rather than an alternative explanation of the pattern.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?
choices: Countries that liberalized their press subsequently improved on governance measures, while comparable countries that did not showed no change
Press freedom rankings are compiled by several independent organizations
Governments in high-ranking countries spend more on public administration
Journalists in low-ranking countries face legal restrictions
questions.explanation: A before-and-after comparison with a control group establishes temporal order and rules out the reverse-causation reading. Multiple ranking sources improve measurement without addressing direction.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department's claim?
choices: System logs show average time per case fell by a third after the change
Officers rated the system highly in a satisfaction survey
The system was adopted at every post simultaneously
Training on the system took two days
questions.explanation: Objective logs replace the self-reports that made the original evidence weak. A satisfaction survey is another subjective measure and compounds rather than corrects the problem.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department's claim?
choices: The share of applications found fraudulent fell by half as well
Interview waiting times increased
Applications fell at posts without interview requirements too
Fraud detection methods were unchanged
questions.explanation: A falling fraud rate, as opposed to a falling count, cannot be explained by lower volume. Option {{2}} would weaken the claim by suggesting the volume drop had an unrelated cause.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the section's prediction?
choices: The electoral commission has since been reconstituted on terms the opposition demanded
The opposition's leadership has not changed
Turnout in the previous elections was low
The opposition has limited campaign funding
questions.explanation: If the grievance that motivated the boycotts has been addressed, the basis for repeating them is gone. Unchanged leadership would if anything support the prediction, and turnout and funding bear on outcome rather than participation.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's inference?
choices: The three replacements have each publicly criticized the previous approach
The reshuffle occurred at the usual point in the electoral cycle
The prime minister described the changes as routine
Two other ministers were also moved between portfolios
questions.explanation: Replacements on record against the old approach make a policy motive far more likely than a factional or cosmetic one. Options {{1,2}} point toward routine explanations and would weaken the inference.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the official's claim?
choices: Surveys of attendees show sustained shifts in views on the sponsoring country
Event costs per attendee fell
The events received local press coverage
Attendance grew fastest among students
questions.explanation: Measured attitude change converts an output measure into an outcome measure, which is what the claim of success requires. Cost efficiency and coverage describe the program's operation rather than its effect.

questions.stem: If both the fraud figure and the volume figure are accurate, which is best supported?
choices: Whether the fraud rate changed cannot be determined from the figures given
The interview requirement had no effect
The fraud rate rose
The fraud rate fell
questions.explanation: A count fell and the denominator fell, but neither magnitude is specified precisely enough to fix the ratio's direction. Asserting any change in the rate goes beyond what the two facts jointly establish.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: The record is consistent with both full compliance and absent enforcement
Officers have complied with the standard
The standard is not being enforced
The standard is poorly drafted
questions.explanation: A null disciplinary record cannot distinguish between the two explanations, which is precisely why it is weak evidence. Committing to either reading, as options {{1,2}} do, claims more than the fact supports.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the economist's observation?
choices: Prices for the sampled goods differ substantially between the two countries
The currency will depreciate
The country's exports are uncompetitive
The trading partner's currency is undervalued
questions.explanation: The price comparison is what the observation directly establishes; overvaluation is an interpretation requiring further assumptions about tradability and comparability. Options {{1,2}} forecast consequences the data alone cannot support.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: The summit did not produce a communiqué
The summit failed
The parties disagreed on every issue
A communiqué was drafted but rejected
questions.explanation: Only the stated fact is supported; every other option adds an interpretation. Distinguishing what a stimulus says from what it invites you to conclude is the whole exercise here.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: This coalition has lasted longer than the historical average
This coalition will collapse soon
This coalition is unusually stable
Most coalitions collapse before twenty months
questions.explanation: Twenty months exceeds eighteen, which is all that follows. 'Unusually stable' would require knowing the distribution's spread, and option {{3}} confuses a mean with a median.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: The target government has not met two of the specified conditions
The target government intends to meet the remaining conditions
The remaining conditions are more difficult than the first three
Relief will be granted
questions.explanation: Meeting three of five entails not having met the other two, which is arithmetic. Intent, relative difficulty, and the outcome are all beyond what the stimulus states.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: Interest payments currently consume a modest share of revenue
The debt will remain manageable
The government could borrow substantially more
The debt is denominated in domestic currency
questions.explanation: The stimulus supports only a description of the current ratio. Sustainability, borrowing capacity, and currency composition are forward-looking or additional facts the figure does not supply.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported?
choices: War would impose severe economic costs on both governments
The two governments will not go to war
Economic interdependence prevents war
Neither government wants war
questions.explanation: The premise about ruinous cost is what the stimulus supplies; the prediction is the specialist's inference, which requires the further assumption that governments act on economic calculation. Option {{2}} generalizes a contested claim.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument assumes that:
choices: Exports drove GDP rather than moving with it as one of its components
Imports remained constant
Export prices were stable
GDP is measured at constant prices
questions.explanation: Since exports are part of GDP, their co-movement is nearly guaranteed and cannot establish direction. The argument needs the causal premise that options {{1,2}} do not supply.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument assumes that:
choices: The next crisis will resemble the last three in its origins
Exchange rate data are published promptly
Currency instability is easy to detect
Other indicators are more expensive to monitor
questions.explanation: Efficiency depends on the indicator predicting the crisis that actually arrives, which requires similarity to past cases. The other options concern feasibility and cost rather than whether the indicator will work.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument assumes that:
choices: The stations observers visited were representative of all polling stations
Observers were impartial
Voting was conducted by secret ballot
Turnout was high
questions.explanation: Generalizing from a visited subset to the whole election requires representativeness. Impartiality matters for the accuracy of the observations made, but even perfectly impartial observers cannot report on stations they did not visit.

questions.stem: The department's argument assumes that:
choices: Assessment scores predict conduct
Participants took the assessment seriously
The assessment was administered fairly
Corruption is a serious problem in the department
questions.explanation: Effectiveness means changed behavior, so the score must stand in for conduct. Fair administration and serious participation would make the scores accurate measures of knowledge without connecting knowledge to behavior.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument assumes that:
choices: Bilateral activity comes at the expense of multilateral engagement
Bilateral agreements are easier to negotiate
Multilateral institutions were once more effective
States prefer bilateral arrangements
questions.explanation: The inference from more bilateral agreements to multilateral decline requires that the two trade off. States can and do expand both simultaneously, which the argument never rules out.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument assumes that:
choices: A party that finds the text unacceptable would have said so during consultation
All parties attended the consultations
The text has not been revised
Consultations were conducted in a common language
questions.explanation: Reading silence as acceptance requires that objections would surface when available. Option {{1}} is a necessary condition for even hearing an objection, but the deeper assumption is about whether parties would voice one.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: Majority support is sufficient to justify a policy
The polling was methodologically sound
The majority is well informed
Opponents will accept the outcome
questions.explanation: The argument moves from popularity straight to justification, which requires that popularity settle the question. Sound polling would establish that the support is real without establishing that it justifies anything.

questions.stem: The department's projection assumes that:
choices: Applicants elsewhere will adopt the digital system at rates comparable to the pilot population
The system will not require maintenance
Staff will need no additional training
Processing time is the only relevant measure
questions.explanation: Extrapolating the pilot's 40 percent requires comparable uptake, which a highly connected urban sample makes doubtful. Maintenance and training are implementation costs rather than threats to the projection's logic.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: The proposed policy's drawbacks are less serious than those of the alternatives
All alternatives have been identified
Doing nothing is not an option
The drawbacks cannot be mitigated
questions.explanation: Adoption follows only if the proposal compares favorably, which the argument never establishes. Options {{1,2}} identify additional gaps, but the comparative premise is what the conclusion directly requires.

questions.stem: The delegation's argument assumes that:
choices: The other two positions define a reasonable range
The other parties negotiated independently
Its own position was formulated first
Moderation is desirable in negotiation
questions.explanation: A midpoint is moderate only if the endpoints are themselves within reason; between two extremes lies a third extreme. Option {{3}} concerns whether moderation is worth claiming, not whether the claim is warranted.

questions.stem: Which additional premise would allow the conclusion that some working group members have doctoral degrees?
choices: The working group's economists are department economists
All department staff have doctoral degrees
Some economists lack doctoral degrees
The working group includes non-economists
questions.explanation: The gap is that the second premise covers department economists while the first covers working group economists; identifying the two closes it. Option {{1}} would work too but is far stronger than needed, and a correct answer should be the minimal bridging premise.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most help determine whether inflation fell in Country K?
choices: Country K's inflation data for the past three years
The number of countries that adopted the reform
The average inflation decline among adopters
Whether Country K's neighbors adopted the reform
questions.explanation: The question is about a particular country, and only its own data answers it. Aggregate statistics about adopters sharpen the general expectation without resolving whether K is among the majority.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most undermine the force of the conclusion about the fisheries agreement?
choices: The relevant government is not expected to change
Some agreements reached without time pressure have also collapsed
The fisheries agreement is unusually detailed
Time pressure is common in negotiations
questions.explanation: The premise conditions collapse on a change of government, so if none is expected the prediction has no occasion to operate. The other options leave the conditional untouched.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most weaken any expectation that the pending treaty will be ratified?
choices: Several treaties with bipartisan sponsorship have also been rejected
The Senate has rejected few treaties overall
Bipartisan sponsorship has become more common
The pending treaty is lengthy
questions.explanation: The premise establishes only that rejected treaties lacked sponsorship; showing that sponsored treaties are also rejected severs any inference from sponsorship to success. Option {{1}} would if anything raise the base rate of ratification.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the adviser's argument?
choices: Agencies are legally required to follow procedures that firms may disregard
Some private firms are inefficient
Government salaries are lower than private sector salaries
Performance management systems vary widely among firms
questions.explanation: It identifies a structural source of the efficiency gap that management practices cannot remove, so importing those practices would not close it. Option {{1}} is a quibble that leaves the general comparison intact.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the officer's assessment?
choices: The source's reporting has been independently corroborated on four separate occasions
The source has reported for many years
The source has no known political affiliation
The information is consistent with the officer's expectations
questions.explanation: Repeated independent corroboration converts a single instance into a pattern established by outside evidence. Option {{3}} would weaken confidence, since agreement with prior expectations invites confirmation bias.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the adviser's position?
choices: The current assessment rests on the same analytic method that produced the earlier error
The earlier assessment concerned a different country
The assessment team has been reorganized
Assessments are reviewed before distribution
questions.explanation: A shared flawed method connects the past failure to the present product, turning a weak ad hominem into a substantive objection. Options {{1,2}} both cut the other way by distancing the current assessment from the earlier one.

questions.stem: Which of the following most closely parallels the officer's reasoning?
choices: Defendants usually plead not guilty, so this defendant's plea tells us nothing about guilt
This witness lied once, so nothing the witness says can be believed
Most reports are accurate, so this report is accurate
The allegation is serious, so it is probably true
questions.explanation: Both move from a general behavioral base rate to dismissing a particular statement's evidentiary value — and both are wrong for the same reason: the base rate holds whether or not the particular case is genuine. Option {{1}} is a different error, generalizing from a single instance.

questions.stem: Which of the following most closely parallels the official's reasoning?
choices: We have already paid for the tickets, so we should attend the performance despite the storm warning
The performance received poor reviews, so we should not attend
We enjoyed the last performance, so we should attend this one
Attending would cost more than staying home
questions.explanation: Both treat an unrecoverable prior expenditure as a reason to proceed, ignoring the forward-looking comparison. The remaining options each reason from expected outcomes, which is the correct form.

questions.stem: Which of the following most closely parallels the adviser's reasoning?
choices: The smoke alarm has never sounded, so it must be working
The smoke alarm sounded, so there is a fire
The alarm is new, so it is reliable
The alarm was tested last week and worked
questions.explanation: Both treat the absence of an alert as evidence of function, when a dead device produces the identical record. Option {{3}} describes the test that would actually distinguish the two possibilities.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the department's inference?
choices: A compliance record is informative only where a functioning detection mechanism exists
Conduct standards should be reviewed periodically
Discipline should be proportionate to the violation
Officers should be trained on new standards
questions.explanation: The principle conditions the record's evidentiary value on detection, which the department never establishes. The other options concern how standards should be administered rather than what a null record shows.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's claim?
choices: A program should be judged by its effect on its intended outcome, not by participation levels
Outreach events should be held quarterly
Programs should be evaluated by external reviewers
Attendance should be recorded accurately
questions.explanation: Attendance is the official's entire evidence, and this principle disqualifies it as a measure of success. Option {{3}} would improve the accuracy of a metric that the principle says is the wrong one.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the commentator's conclusion?
choices: Regional experience is indispensable to effective performance as an ambassador
Ambassadors should be career officers
Nominees should be confirmed by the Senate
Language ability should be required for all diplomatic posts
questions.explanation: Only a principle making regional experience indispensable turns its absence into disqualification. The other options concern selection procedure or a different qualification, neither of which supports this particular argument.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the commentator's argument?
choices: Applying different principles to materially different situations is consistent rather than incoherent
Foreign policy should prioritize national interest
States should apply the same rule to allies and adversaries
Self-determination is a settled principle of international law
questions.explanation: The charge of incoherence assumes the two cases are alike, and this principle denies that differing treatment of differing cases is inconsistent. Option {{2}} would support the commentator instead.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the researcher's argument?
choices: An institution is legitimate if its rulings are generally accepted as authoritative, whether or not compliance is costly in each case
International courts should have compulsory jurisdiction
States should comply with all rulings
Legitimacy requires democratic accountability
questions.explanation: It replaces the researcher's demanding standard with one most legal systems satisfy, removing the basis for the conclusion. Option {{2}} restates an ideal without addressing what legitimacy requires.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the negotiator's inference?
choices: A party that hardens its position without new substantive justification is responding to pressures outside the negotiation
Negotiators should always explain position changes
Domestic politics shapes all foreign policy
Hardened positions indicate bad faith
questions.explanation: The principle licenses exactly the inference drawn — from unexplained hardening to external pressure. Option {{2}} is too broad to distinguish this case, and the fourth reaches a different conclusion about motive.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country M will eventually join the trade bloc
Eliminating agricultural tariffs is not sufficient for membership in the trade bloc
Country M meets all requirements for membership
Some bloc members retain agricultural tariffs
questions.explanation: M has done what all members have done yet is not a member, so the action cannot by itself confer membership. Option {{3}} directly contradicts the premise that all members have eliminated those tariffs.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be properly concluded?
choices: The department will fund the literacy project
The literacy project has satisfied a necessary condition for funding
The literacy project is more likely to be funded than unevaluated projects
The department funds all evaluated projects
questions.explanation: 'Only if' marks evaluation as necessary, not sufficient, so meeting it establishes eligibility and nothing more. Option {{0}} affirms the consequent; the third makes a probabilistic claim that a statement of logical necessity does not support.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true?
choices: Country R has not ratified the protocol
Country R will be sanctioned
Country R intends to ratify the protocol later
Ratifying the protocol prevents emissions from rising
questions.explanation: No ratifier has been permitted to increase its allocation, and R has been permitted, so R cannot be a ratifier — a valid contrapositive. Option {{3}} confuses a restriction on allocations with a claim about actual emissions.

questions.stem: The official's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that:
choices: Officers who volunteer for hardship posts may differ from those who would be compelled to serve
Hardship posts are more expensive to staff
Career satisfaction is difficult to measure
Some officers have medical restrictions
questions.explanation: The evidence comes from officers who chose hardship service, and the proposal would apply to everyone. Whatever disposition led volunteers to go may be the same thing producing their satisfaction, in which case compelling the unwilling would not reproduce it.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Compliance will certainly improve within a year
Based on the past pattern, compliance can reasonably be expected to improve
Publishing findings is the only way to improve compliance
Compliance would not have improved without publication
questions.explanation: An unbroken past record supports an expectation, not a guarantee — the stimulus reports what has happened rather than stating a rule. Options {{2,3}} treat a sufficient condition as though it were necessary.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?
choices: Fuel subsidies had been in place for over a decade
A large coal-fired plant on the city's edge closed permanently in the same month
Subsidy removal was unpopular with urban residents
Air quality is measured at three monitoring stations
questions.explanation: A separate major emissions source disappearing at the same time supplies an alternative cause sufficient to explain the improvement on its own. Popularity and the age of the subsidy bear on the politics, not on the causal question.

questions.stem: The director's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: Competitive admission means graduates already outperformed others before enrolling
The certification examination may be poorly designed
Some graduates do not take the examination
Non-graduates may have studied independently
questions.explanation: Selecting entrants on prior examination scores guarantees the graduate pool is stronger at the outset, so the later gap may reflect admissions rather than instruction. The final sentence of the stimulus is placed there as the signal.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is flawed because it:
choices: Treats the absence of fighting as evidence that the cause of the fighting has ended
Relies on an arbitrarily chosen six-month period
Assumes ceasefires are always formally negotiated
Ignores the role of external mediators
questions.explanation: A ceasefire suspends hostilities; it is entirely compatible with an unresolved dispute held in check by exhaustion or deterrence. Option {{1}} identifies a lesser weakness — the inference would fail at any duration, because cessation and resolution are different things.

questions.stem: If the auditor's observation is accurate, the reported coverage figure is unreliable because:
choices: The denominator understates the current target population
Vaccination records may be incomplete
Migration makes the campaign harder to administer
Census data are collected for other purposes
questions.explanation: Coverage is doses divided by population; a twelve-year-old count taken before substantial migration is too small a denominator, which inflates the percentage. The error is arithmetic, not administrative.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument assumes that:
choices: Prosecution volume is a valid indicator of the agency's effectiveness
The agency has adequate funding
Corruption is more prevalent than official figures suggest
The agency's staff are competent
questions.explanation: The inference works only if fewer prosecutions means worse performance — yet a successful deterrent would reduce the offenses available to prosecute, producing the same decline. Without that assumption the evidence is equally consistent with the opposite conclusion.

questions.stem: The colleague's observation undermines the diplomat's claim by suggesting that:
choices: The communiqué produced no change in any party's position
The parties negotiated in bad faith
The summit was too short to accomplish anything
Communiqués are not legally binding
questions.explanation: If the text restates commitments already made publicly, signing it added nothing, so unanimity is not evidence of accomplishment. The observation speaks to the substance of the outcome rather than to the parties' sincerity.

questions.stem: The administrator's conclusion is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Students who study abroad may differ in family resources and prior attainment
Salaries vary widely by field of study
A decade is too short a period to assess earnings
Some study-abroad programs are more rigorous than others
questions.explanation: Study abroad is not randomly distributed; it correlates with wealth and academic standing, both of which independently predict later earnings. Expanding access to students unlike the current participants would not necessarily reproduce the earnings gap.

questions.stem: The official's proposal assumes that:
choices: Administrative efficiency is the appropriate basis for choosing grant size
Small grants have never achieved their objectives
Large grantees are more experienced
Administrative costs will continue to rise
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a cost ratio straight to a funding decision, which requires that cost-per-dollar be the deciding criterion. Small grants may reach recipients large grants cannot, and the argument never addresses what the money accomplishes.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, most supports the civil liberties group's position?
choices: Security programs should be discontinued whenever they are controversial
A program that restricts liberty is justified only if less restrictive means would not have achieved the same result
Intelligence methods should be disclosed to the public
Disrupting plots is the primary measure of a security program's value
questions.explanation: The group's objection is precisely that the necessity of the intrusive method has not been demonstrated, which this least-restrictive-means principle makes decisive. Option {{3}} supports the security service instead, and the first is a much weaker principle the group never invoked.

questions.stem: The specialist's reasoning is most vulnerable because:
choices: The change of government may have coincided with other shifts that made negotiation possible
Formal negotiations are often preceded by informal contacts
Governments change for many reasons
The specialist has not identified which government changed
questions.explanation: Sequence is not cause: altered economic conditions, external pressure, or a shift in the other state's position could have made talks possible at that moment regardless of the personnel change. Option {{1}} is true and mildly relevant but does not identify the inferential error.

questions.stem: The donor's recommendation is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Clinic B may achieve its rate by treating less severe cases
Clinic A employs more staff
Recovery rates fluctuate month to month
Clinic B is smaller and may lack capacity to expand
questions.explanation: Case mix is the standard confound in outcome comparisons: a clinic handling milder presentations will post a higher recovery rate without performing better. Option {{3}} is a real practical concern but concedes the comparison; the first challenges whether it means anything.

questions.stem: The policy paper's reasoning is flawed because it:
choices: Treats a feature common to past successes as a requirement for future ones
Relies on too few cases
Does not define democratic transition
Ignores transitions outside the region
questions.explanation: That every success shared a feature does not establish the feature is necessary — growth may have been incidental, or the successful cases may simply be a biased sample of the conditions under which transitions are attempted. Option {{1}} is a lesser version of the same complaint.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the officer's conclusion?
choices: The new front office substantially revised cables before transmission
The template was adopted at several other posts
Washington's rating scale was unchanged
The officer helped design the template
questions.explanation: If a second change introduced at the same moment directly altered the product being rated, the improvement is attributable to it rather than to the template. Option {{3}} raises bias but leaves the evidence itself untouched.

questions.stem: The information about vehicle registrations undermines the ministry's claim by suggesting that:
choices: Fatalities may have fallen because there were fewer vehicles on the road
The fuel price increase was more unpopular than the campaign
Traffic fatalities are poorly recorded
The campaign was too short to have an effect
questions.explanation: Registrations fell by more than fatalities did, so exposure to risk dropped at least as fast as the outcome — the fatality rate per vehicle may not have improved at all. The comparison of the two percentages is what carries the objection.

questions.stem: The negotiator's argument assumes that:
choices: The other side's circumstances and alternatives have not materially changed since the earlier talks
The other side negotiates in good faith
The earlier agreement was fully implemented
Both sides value the agreement equally
questions.explanation: Comparing offers across three years is informative only if what the other side can obtain elsewhere has held steady; a party with better alternatives now will reject terms it once accepted. The comparison is to a moving baseline unless that assumption holds.

questions.stem: The analyst's recommendation is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: Countries that sign such treaties may already be those investors find attractive
Investment treaties constrain domestic regulatory authority
Not all foreign investment benefits recipients
Treaty texts vary considerably
questions.explanation: Governments that pursue investment treaties are typically those already reforming to court capital, so the treaty may be a marker of investor-friendly policy rather than its cause. Options {{1,2}} raise reasons the policy might be undesirable, which is a separate question from whether the evidence supports it.

questions.stem: The director's response is weak because:
choices: An absence of detected incidents does not establish that procedures are adequate
Eleven years is a short period
Written procedures are required by regulation
The inspector general has broader authority than the director
questions.explanation: Without a procedure, there may also be no reliable means of detecting or recording an incident — so the clean record may reflect the same gap it is offered to excuse. Appeals to authority and to regulation, as in options {{2,3}}, sidestep the reasoning rather than addressing it.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Treats a failure to detect an effect as a demonstration that no effect exists
Relies on evaluators who may be biased
Ignores the program's administrative costs
Assumes household income is the only relevant outcome
questions.explanation: A study lacking the sample size or duration to detect a modest effect returns a null result whether or not the effect is real. Option {{3}} is also a genuine gap, but the inferential error — reading absence of evidence as evidence of absence — is the primary one.

questions.stem: The adviser's argument is weakest in that it:
choices: Generalizes from three cases without considering how many private-sector appointees were ineffective
Assumes ambassadorial effectiveness can be ranked
Ignores the role of career officers
Does not define private-sector experience
questions.explanation: Looking only at the successes tells you nothing about the base rate: if a hundred business appointees served and three excelled, the record argues against the proposal. Selecting on the outcome and reasoning backward is the structural error.

questions.stem: The projection's stated assumption is questionable primarily because:
choices: Taxpayers commonly adjust reported income and timing in response to rate changes
Revenue projections are inherently uncertain
The reform may not be enacted
Six percent is a small increase
questions.explanation: Behavioral response is the central difficulty in revenue estimation — static scoring assumes it away by construction. Option {{1}} is true of all forecasts and identifies nothing specific to this one.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion confuses:
choices: The incidence of corruption with the reporting of corruption
Correlation with sample size
Press freedom with press quality
Government corruption with private corruption
questions.explanation: A free press detects and publicizes corruption that an unfree press conceals, so more reports may indicate better observation rather than more wrongdoing. Measurement intensity varying with the very condition under study is a recurring trap in cross-country comparison.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the economic section's observation?
choices: The host country's economy is not actually growing
The reported figures are implausibly stable for an economy of this kind
The host government is deliberately falsifying data
Growth is lower than 7 percent
questions.explanation: The evidence is about the improbable smoothness of the series, which supports doubting the figures without establishing what the true numbers are or why they differ. Options {{0,2,3}} each specify a conclusion the observation cannot reach.

questions.stem: The official's argument overlooks the possibility that:
choices: The department may decline to bring cases it expects to lose
The arbitration panel may be biased
Some cases settle before hearing
The department has brought few cases
questions.explanation: Selective case selection produces a perfect record regardless of the quality of the underlying positions — the unbrought cases are exactly the weak ones. Options {{2,3}} gesture at the same territory but do not name the mechanism that makes the record uninformative.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the study's attribution?
choices: Officers who remain past three years are disproportionately assigned to lower-risk applicant pools
Refusal rates vary across posts
Local knowledge is difficult to quantify
Some officers extend their tours voluntarily
questions.explanation: If longer-serving officers see systematically different applicants, the refusal gap reflects caseload rather than judgment. The other options raise measurement and selection issues without supplying a competing explanation of the specific difference observed.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it:
choices: Assumes that what governments judge to be in their interest is in fact beneficial
Ignores the role of domestic legislatures in ratification
Assumes both governments had equal bargaining power
Overlooks the interests of third countries
questions.explanation: The inference slides from 'each government believed it was benefiting' to 'the agreement is beneficial' — governments can misjudge, and the interests they pursue may not be those of their populations. Options {{2,3}} are real considerations but neither closes the gap the argument depends on.

questions.stem: The proposed measure assumes that:
choices: The number of agreements concluded reflects the value of an embassy's work
All embassies have equal opportunity to conclude agreements
Agreements are always implemented
questions.explanation: A count-based metric requires both that agreements track value and that posts are comparable on the dimension being counted — an embassy in a small state with few bilateral questions will score poorly however well it performs. Either assumption alone leaves the measure open to the other objection.

questions.stem: The evaluation's comparison is unreliable because:
choices: Villages able to contribute 20 percent of costs likely differ in wealth and organization
Sanitation outcomes were self-reported
The project period was too short
Non-participating villages may have received other assistance
questions.explanation: The cost-share requirement screens for exactly the characteristics that independently predict better sanitation, so the two groups were never comparable. Option {{3}} would weaken the finding but is speculative; the selection mechanism is stated in the stimulus.

questions.stem: The analyst's argument is flawed because the polls:
choices: Sample a population selected in a way that guarantees a favorable result
Were conducted too far before the election
Do not report a margin of error
May have been conducted by inexperienced staff
questions.explanation: Voters who visit a party's own website to register a preference are overwhelmingly its supporters, so the sample cannot represent the electorate. This is self-selection at its most extreme, and no methodological refinement of the other kinds would repair it.

questions.stem: The official's argument assumes that:
choices: Holding the required certification indicates sufficient practical language ability
All officers wish to serve in language-designated positions
The certification examination is administered annually
Language training is the department's largest training expense
questions.explanation: The argument treats a credential as evidence of capability, which holds only if the credential measures what the job requires. If the examination is easier than the work, full certification and inadequate ability are entirely compatible.

questions.stem: The researcher's conclusion is questionable because:
choices: States may pursue interests other than direct physical exposure, such as commercial or reputational advantage
Climate risk is difficult to measure
Vocal advocacy is not the same as effective advocacy
Some exposed countries are also vocal
questions.explanation: The argument equates self-interest with exposure to physical harm, but a state may gain economically from a policy transition or seek standing as a norm entrepreneur. Ruling out one form of interest does not rule out interest as such.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the evaluator's observation?
choices: Audits should never be required of grantees
The audit requirement screens on organizational size rather than on merit
Small organizations are less accountable than large ones
The donor should fund only large organizations
questions.explanation: A requirement that the smallest organizations cannot afford filters by capacity to comply, not by quality of work. Options {{0,3}} leap to policy recommendations the observation alone does not justify, and the third reverses the point.

questions.stem: The commentator's argument confuses:
choices: The imposition of costs with the achievement of the policy objective
Economic damage with humanitarian harm
Multilateral with unilateral sanctions
Short-term with long-term effects
questions.explanation: Sanctions aim to change behavior; damage is the instrument, not the goal. A target that absorbs severe costs without conceding has defeated the policy, however much harm was inflicted — which is why the inference fails.

questions.stem: The officer's argument is flawed because it:
choices: Attacks the source of the assessment rather than its substance
Assumes family connections are always disclosed
Overlooks the colleague's professional record
Relies on an unverified claim about the connections
questions.explanation: This is an ad hominem: the colleague's ties might warrant scrutiny of the analysis, but they establish nothing about whether it is correct. Family connections could as easily be a source of insight as of bias, which is why they cannot substitute for engaging the argument.

questions.stem: The change in survey method matters because:
choices: Differences in mode can shift responses independently of any change in actual trust
Telephone surveys are always less accurate
The sample size may have changed
Respondents may have forgotten the initiative
questions.explanation: Respondents answer sensitive questions differently by telephone than face to face, so any part of the 9-point movement may be an artifact of measurement. Option {{1}} overstates it — the problem is that the two waves are not comparable, not that one method is inferior.

questions.stem: The specialist's argument is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: The war preceding the organization's founding may explain the subsequent peace
The organization has other functions besides preventing war
Member states have had disputes short of war
The organization's membership has changed over time
questions.explanation: A decisive war that settled the territorial questions removes the principal cause of fighting, so peace may be the legacy of the settlement rather than the achievement of the organization. The final sentence of the stimulus supplies this alternative explanation directly.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most undermine the official's proposal?
choices: Programs should be evaluated by what they accomplish rather than by what they cost to administer
Administrative costs should be minimized wherever possible
Grant decisions should be made by technical experts
Donors should support a diverse portfolio of grantees
questions.explanation: The proposal rests entirely on an administrative cost ratio, so a principle subordinating cost to accomplishment removes its only support. Option {{3}} also cuts against the proposal but on narrower grounds — it would permit concentration if diversity were otherwise satisfied.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the commentator's conclusion?
choices: A program should be judged a failure unless rigorous evaluation demonstrates a measurable benefit
Programs should be continued until proven harmful
Evaluation methods should be chosen by independent experts
Household income is the best measure of development impact
questions.explanation: The commentator treats the absence of demonstrated effect as sufficient for a verdict of failure, which only a principle placing the burden of proof on the program can license. Option {{1}} states the opposite presumption, and the fourth supports the choice of outcome without addressing the burden.

questions.stem: Which principle, if accepted, would most support the official's proposal?
choices: Personnel policies should maximize aggregate career satisfaction even where individual preferences differ
Officers should be consulted before assignment policies change
Hardship posts should receive additional resources
Career satisfaction should be measured annually
questions.explanation: The proposal would compel service that officers might not choose, so it needs a principle permitting aggregate benefit to override individual preference. Option {{1}} would obstruct the proposal, and the third and fourth are administrative measures that leave the mandate unjustified.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the director's conclusion?
choices: Among applicants with identical admission scores, those admitted outperform those turned away
The institute has operated for twenty years
Graduates report high satisfaction with the curriculum
The certification examination is nationally standardized
questions.explanation: Comparing candidates matched on the selection variable removes the admissions advantage, so a remaining gap is attributable to the institute. Satisfaction and program longevity say nothing about whether the instruction caused the performance difference.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the exchange described?
choices: The surveillance program disrupted no plots
The necessity of the program has not been established by the evidence cited
Conventional methods are always sufficient
The security service acted unlawfully
questions.explanation: The civil liberties group disputes what the four disruptions prove, not that they occurred, so what remains open is necessity. Options {{0,2,3}} each assert something neither party has established.

questions.stem: The economic section's argument depends on the assumption that:
choices: Genuine growth in an economy of this kind would show more year-to-year variation
The host government has a motive to misreport
Other economies in the region report lower growth
International organizations have questioned the figures
questions.explanation: The inference runs entirely from implausible smoothness, which requires that real economies of this type fluctuate. Motive and third-party doubts would make the suspicion more compelling but are not what the stated reasoning rests on.

questions.stem: Which of the following must be true if the evaluator's observation is accurate?
choices: Some organizations capable of performing well are excluded from funding by the audit requirement
Audited organizations perform better than unaudited ones
The donor is indifferent to local rootedness
Audit costs exceed the value of small grants
questions.explanation: If the requirement is binding on the smallest and most locally rooted organizations, at least some competent applicants are screened out — this follows directly. The other options add claims about performance, motive, and cost that the observation does not establish.

questions.stem: If both the ministry's figure and the registration figure are accurate, which is best supported?
choices: The campaign had no effect whatsoever
Fatalities per registered vehicle did not fall and may have risen
The fuel price increase was intended as a safety measure
Traffic fatalities will rise again next year
questions.explanation: Registrations fell 22 percent while fatalities fell 18 percent, so the ratio moved unfavorably. Option {{0}} overstates the case — a modest campaign effect could still be hidden inside these aggregates, which is exactly why the raw decline proves nothing.
